title: Target Sums With Unlimited Reuse
statement:
You get a list parts of distinct positive integers and a positive integer target. Return every combination of parts whose sum is exactly target. Each part may be used any number of times.

A combination is a multiset: two combinations are the same if they use every part the same number of times, whatever the order. Return each combination once. The combinations may come in any order, and the numbers inside one may also be in any order. If nothing works, return an empty list.

examples.why: 3 + 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 + 3 are the same combination. A search that may pick any part at every step finds it three times.
Reuse is what makes both work. Using each part at most once finds nothing, since 2 + 7 = 9 and 2 + 5 + 7 = 14.
Every part is already bigger than the target.

constraints: All values in parts are distinct
hints: Without care, 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 are both found. How can you make sure every combination is built in only one order?
Build each combination in a fixed order: once you move past a part, never go back to it. That is the start index from the plain subsets search.

Recurse with (start, remaining). Loop i from start; choose parts[i] and recurse with start = i, not i + 1, so the same part can be taken again. Stop a branch when remaining hits 0 (record) or goes below 0. Sorting lets you break the loop as soon as a part is too big.

explain.intuition:
This is the same template as listing subsets, with two changes. First, a node is an answer only when the sum left to reach is exactly 0, and a branch dies as soon as it goes below 0. Second, reuse: in the subsets search a child recurses with i + 1, which moves past the number just taken. Here it recurses with i, so the same part stays available, but nothing to its left does.

That start index is what kills repeated orders. Every combination is built in one fixed order (by position in the list), so 3, 3, 5 is built and 5, 3, 3 never is, since after taking 5 the search can no longer go back to 3. If you sort the parts first, you also get cheap pruning: once a part is bigger than what is left, every part after it is too, so the loop can stop.
steps: go(start, left): if left === 0, record a copy of cur and return.
Loop i from start. If parts[i] > left, break: the rest are bigger still.
Choose parts[i], call go(i, left - parts[i]) (start stays at i to allow reuse), un-choose.
pitfalls: Recursing with go(0, …). Every order of the same parts is built, as in the first example.
Recursing with go(i + 1, …). That forbids reuse, so [5, 5] in the second example is lost.
Breaking on a too-big part without sorting first. A smaller part later in the list is then never tried.

complexity.time: Exponential: O(n^(T/m)) branches in the worst case, T = target, m = smallest part

solutions.title: Take the part again, or move on
solutions.idea: At each step there are two choices: use parts[i] once more (stay on i), or never use it again (go to i + 1). A path ends when the sum left is 0 or the parts run out.

solutions.title: Loop from the start index, sorted, with pruning
solutions.idea: The subsets template, recursing with start = i so a part can repeat. Sorting lets the loop stop at the first part that does not fit.

followups: Only the number of combinations is needed, for a target up to 10 000. Which dynamic-programming loop counts them without listing them, and why must the loop over parts be the outer one?
Each combination may now use at most k parts in total. Where does that limit go in the search?
